source: NCERT Class XI, Indian Constitution at Work, Ch. 9 (Constitution as a Living Document).

sections.heading: 1. A Living Document
points: The Constitution is a **'living document'** — it can grow and change with the times, not a fixed, rigid text.
It has endured because it **balances stability with flexibility** and is periodically **amended and reinterpreted**.
Its makers deliberately made it capable of adapting to new needs.

sections.heading: 2. Amendment of the Constitution (Art 368)
points: The Constitution can be amended under **Article 368**; three types of procedure:

sub: By **simple majority** (some provisions, like admission of states — not under Art 368).
By **special majority** (2/3 of members present and voting + majority of total membership).
By special majority **plus ratification by half the state legislatures** (for federal provisions).

points: Over 100 amendments have been made — showing flexibility.

sections.heading: 3. Judicial Interpretation and Basic Structure
points: The Constitution also evolves through **judicial interpretation** (courts reinterpret provisions over time).

The **Basic Structure Doctrine** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) — Parliament can amend but **cannot destroy the basic structure** (e.g. supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, secularism, judicial review, federalism).
This doctrine balances **parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy**.

sections.heading: 4. Examples of Evolution
points: Major amendments: **42nd (1976)** — Fundamental Duties, added 'socialist, secular, integrity' to Preamble; **44th (1978)** — restored balance after Emergency; **73rd/74th (1992)** — local government; **86th (2002)** — Right to Education; **101st (2016)** — GST.
The interplay of **legislature, judiciary and public opinion** keeps the Constitution alive.
The Constitution thus remains relevant across changing times.

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Constitution = living document (balances stability + flexibility).
Amendment under Art 368: simple majority, special majority, special + state ratification.
Basic Structure Doctrine = Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
42nd Amendment (1976) = added Fundamental Duties + secular/socialist to Preamble.
101st Amendment (2016) = GST.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: The Constitution is amended under **Article 368** (three procedures).
Parliament **cannot alter the 'basic structure'** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added the words **socialist, secular, integrity** to the Preamble.
The Constitution evolves through **amendment AND judicial interpretation**.
